clue.text: When elevated turnover in battery production usually occurs?

definitions.text: When elevated turnover in battery production usually occurs?

blocks.note: surface reading: stock rotation in a factory making electrical cells
setter's reading: tossing something flat into the air and flipping it while cooking batter

explanation.surface: A question about when stock in a battery factory is moved on fastest.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'battery' as batter-y: things made from batter are flipped high in the pan, and the day for doing that is Shrove Tuesday, before Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday is the traditional day in Britain for making and tossing flat batter cakes in a frying pan.

clue.text: Frantic plug propped up former conference centre

indicators.note: in a down entry, something propped up is raised from below, so the letters read bottom to top

explanation.surface: A crazed bung holding something up, with a nod to a historic meeting place.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1945 Potsdam Conference, near Berlin, is where the Allied leaders settled post-war Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: The German city hosted the Allied summit of Churchill/Attlee, Truman and Stalin in 1945.

clue.text: Reduced fare that's only natural?

blocks.note: surface reading: a cut-price ticket on a bus or train
setter's reading: food served in small portions, built on fresh ingredients and light, unadorned flavours

explanation.surface: A discounted ticket price that seems no more than fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fare' and 'reduced' both have a cooking sense: food, and a sauce boiled down. The modern French style is known for tiny portions and natural flavours.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1970s French cooking movement favoured small, light plates and fresh produce over heavy sauces.

clue.text: Most of dish overturned, regrettably

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept
something overturned is upside down, so in a down entry the letters run the other way

explanation.surface: Someone sadly reports that a bowl of food has mostly been knocked over.
explanation.definitionFit: The interjection expresses sorrow or regret, so it can stand for 'unfortunately' at the head of a sentence.

clue.text: Prophet from Israel is hampered to some extent

indicators.note: only partly, so the solution is a part of the words that follow the link

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A biblical seer from the Holy Land is somewhat held back.
explanation.definitionFit: He is the Old Testament successor of Elijah, a seer of the northern kingdom in the Books of Kings.

clue.text: Case of unusual half-hearted rogue will grab one in the future

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the next word are used
with half its heart gone, one of the two identical middle letters is dropped
grabbing takes hold of something, so the next piece goes inside

blocks.note: a terror is a troublesome person, as in 'a little terror'

explanation.surface: A tricky case of a reluctant villain who will seize someone later on.
explanation.walkthrough: TERROR has RR at its heart; losing one R leaves TEROR, which takes in I to make TERIOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulterior can mean lying beyond or coming later, so it describes what is still to come; the hidden-motive sense is the usual one.

clue.text: Old ship from Tasmania floundering around Arabia

indicators.note: something floundering around is thrashing about in disorder, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: AR is used as a short form of Arabia

explanation.surface: A vessel from Tasmania struggling somewhere off the Arabian coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The Santa Maria was the flagship of Columbus on his first voyage to the Americas in 1492.

clue.text: Logical philosophy MIT rationalises somehow

indicators.note: somehow says the letters get there in some unspecified way, so they are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: all fifteen letters

explanation.surface: A famous American university makes a reasoned case for some school of thought.
explanation.walkthrough: MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology; the surface makes 'rationalises' sound like part of the logic theme.
explanation.definitionFit: The system of the Greek thinker who founded formal syllogistic reasoning is the classic school of logic.

clue.text: Relative regrets shunning outsiders? False

indicators.note: shunning outsiders means the outermost letters of the phrase are turned away

explanation.surface: A family member regrets keeping strangers away, but it is a lie.
explanation.walkthrough: AUNT RUES loses its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Untrue and false are plain synonyms, both meaning not in accordance with fact.

clue.text: Tense day, pre-noon, before international cataclysm

explanation.surface: A nervous morning ahead of some global disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A giant sea wave set off by an earthquake is a sudden violent upheaval that devastates coasts.

clue.text: Strain is returning in part of joint

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word is read backwards
in places the preceding piece inside the following one

blocks.note: a tenon is the projecting tongue of a mortise-and-tenon joint

explanation.surface: A carpenter's or physio's note that the stress has come back in a joint.
explanation.walkthrough: In a mortise-and-tenon joint, the tenon is the tongue that slots into the hole; 'joint' sounds anatomical but is woodwork.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is stress or stretching force, the same as strain on a rope or on the nerves.

clue.text: Long Parliament's last legislative assembly

indicators.note: last points to the final letter of the possessive word just before it

blocks.note: to be dying for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A reference to the Long Parliament, the seventeenth-century English assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long Parliament' looks like a single historical name, but 'Long' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: A diet is a formal national or imperial parliament, as in the Diet of Worms or Japan's Diet.

clue.text: Article back in forge splitting beam accordingly

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its final letter is used
splitting means driving in between, so a piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a rafter is a sloping roof beam

explanation.surface: A blacksmith's item put back in the forge and cleaving a timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back in forge' looks like returning something to the fire, but it only means the word's tail end; 'accordingly' is an older sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Thereafter can mean 'in accordance with that', an older sense matching accordingly, besides its usual 'after that'.

clue.text: Post free coupon at centre in Wick

indicators.note: letters set free are loosened from their order and can be rearranged
the centre of a word is its middle letters only

explanation.surface: Mail a complimentary voucher to a town in the far north of Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Wick is a town in Caithness; 'Post' looks like a verb but is a noun meaning a job.
explanation.definitionFit: A post is a job or position, and an occupation is likewise a person's employment.

clue.text: Loiter around large lizard

indicators.note: around means one piece goes about the other, enclosing it

blocks.note: to mooch is to hang about aimlessly

explanation.surface: Hang about near a big reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: The moloch, or thorny devil, is a spiny Australian lizard; 'large' looks like it describes the lizard but supplies a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The moloch is a spiky desert reptile of Australia, also called the thorny devil.

clue.text: It's comical to inhale animatedly

indicators.note: doing something animatedly means with lively movement, so the letters jump about

explanation.surface: Someone finds it funny to breathe in with gusto.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolanthe is a Gilbert and Sullivan comic opera, so the work itself is a comedy.

clue.text: Confuse medical field on way to approach problem

blocks.note: ear, nose and throat, a hospital department
an angle is a viewpoint or line of attack

explanation.surface: A doctor's speciality being muddled while tackling a difficult case.
explanation.definitionFit: To entangle is to make tangled or complicated, so to muddle or perplex.

clue.text: Cuban cheat, saving skin, distracted African once

indicators.note: saving the skin means sparing the outside, so only the inner letters are kept
distracted means scattered and confused, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A Caribbean swindler, escaping a beating, puts off someone from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Bechuanaland was the colonial name of Botswana, so a Bechuana was a native of that territory.
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for a Tswana person, from the former British protectorate now Botswana.

clue.text: Ignore report of extra ticket

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the words are judged by how they are spoken

blocks.note: in cricket a bye is an extra run, not scored off the bat

explanation.surface: Disregard news of a spare admission ticket.
explanation.walkthrough: A bye is a run conceded without the ball touching the bat, one of the extras in cricket scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: To bypass something is to go round it, so to sidestep or disregard it.

clue.text: Bowl over that badly breaks cricket bat

indicators.note: breaks means bursting into the middle of something, so a piece goes inside

blocks.note: to bowl over someone is to amaze them

explanation.surface: A ball delivered so poorly that it cracks the batsman's bat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl over' sounds like cricket, but means to impress hugely.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket bats are traditionally made from the wood of a tree of that name, so it is metonymy.

clue.text: Duck away from target catching front of gammy leg

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter
catching means taking hold of something, which ends up enclosed

blocks.note: a shot wide of the mark misses
in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side

explanation.surface: Someone dodging a missile while nursing a lame limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' looks like a verb, but it is the bird. Gammy is British slang for lame.
explanation.definitionFit: The widgeon (also wigeon) is a species of dabbling wildfowl, a kind of freshwater duck.

clue.text: Moon landing initially fills screen in colour

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word before it
filling something means going inside it

blocks.note: Io is a moon of Jupiter
to vet is to screen or check

explanation.surface: The first moon landing broadcast across a TV screen in colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moon landing' reads as one event, but the moon is a specific satellite of Jupiter and 'landing' just supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Violet is the bluish-purple shade at the end of the visible spectrum.

clue.text: Criminal Mafia practice, shunning decree, sufficient to bring on a charge

definitions.text: sufficient to bring on a charge

indicators.note: shunning means avoiding, so those letters are left out
criminal means crooked or wrong, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: an act of parliament is a decree

explanation.surface: Mob racketeering, avoiding a court order, gives enough to prosecute.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing ACT from the phrase leaves MAFIAPRICE to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A prima facie case is evidence that, at first sight, is enough to justify a trial unless rebutted.

clue.text: Reversed HGV approximately a metre

indicators.note: reversed means turned back, so the word is read in the other direction

blocks.note: a dray is a heavy cart for goods, especially beer barrels; an HGV is a heavy goods vehicle

explanation.surface: A lorry backed up by roughly a metre.
explanation.definitionFit: The imperial unit is 36 inches, about 0.91 of the metric unit, so it is close to a metre.

clue.text: Bright star's lover? Not half

indicators.note: not half means one half of the word is taken away

explanation.surface: A gossip column asks about a celebrity's boyfriend; 'Not half!' is British slang for 'Very much so!'
explanation.walkthrough: The front half, CASA, is dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares to great brightness before fading back.

clue.text: Beginning to sabotage sickening sport

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A start to undermining an unpleasant pastime.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing or cruising in wind-powered boats is a recognised water sport.

clue.text: Long time stopping row relating to several popes

indicators.note: stopping something plugs a gap in it, so one piece sits inside the other

explanation.surface: A lengthy pause in an argument, perhaps between rival clergy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' suggests an argument but is a line. Thirteen popes have taken the name Leo.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonine describes things connected with a pontiff named Leo, such as the Leonine City in Rome.

clue.text: Converted an alderman, then one of his ancient relatives?

indicators.note: converted means changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A councillor changes, prompting a dig at his primitive forebears.
explanation.walkthrough: An alderman is a senior local councillor. The question mark flags that the early human is a distant relation of everyone, not just him.
explanation.definitionFit: This extinct human species interbred with our ancestors, so it is a remote kinsman of any modern person.
